@@13601856 <h> Monsoon : Predicting an unpredictable climate system ( Special to IANS ) <p> As news both good and bad pours from across India , the monsoon is once again in the limelight . From farmers , scientists and economists to astrologers , the monsoon has a significance unlike any other climate phenomenon in India . <p> The monsoon provides around 80 per cent of the total rainfall in India . Getting monsoon predictions right occupies much attention of the weather department in India so that governments can make adjustments to their policies and prepare for droughts or floods according to the likely rainfall pattern . <p> However , the Asian monsoon , unlike its counterparts in West Africa and Australia , has been characterised by remarkable unpredictability and seasonal changes in wind direction and quantity and location of rain . Climate change due to global warming has added yet another dimension of unreliability to the monsoon . Understanding the timing , duration and intensity of the monsoon is vital if predictions of drought and flood are to be made . <p> Any marginal change , say a @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ may appear to be small but these apparently small variations in the Indian monsoon can influence agricultural production and the stocks and commodities market in a big way . The variability of rainfall on shorter time scales has the biggest impacts . <p> For instance , intense heavy rainfall leads to flooding while the breaks in monsoon for over a week or more lead to water shortage and agricultural drought . Evenly distributed rainfall over the four monsoon months could be referred to as the best monsoon . <p> The variations in seasonal rainfall are often related to weather in other parts of the world , such as El Ni ? o events in the Pacific Ocean . Simulations of future climate generally suggest an increase in monsoon rainfall on a seasonal mean , area-average basis . <p> This is due to the twin drivers of an increasing land-sea thermal contrast , but more importantly due to warming over the Indian Ocean which allows more moisture to be carried to India . Typically , increases in the total rainfall over India may be in the range of 5-10 per cent , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> The current climate models suggest greater variability in monsoon rainfall from year to year in a warmer world . In the future , it is expected that there will be extreme weather events with excessive rainfall in some years with low to very low rainfall in other years . <p> Most importantly , the regions that earlier experienced sufficient rainfall could face droughts while those that experienced lower rainfall could face floods frequently . The Indian summer climate in the coming century looks to be wetter on average , together with flood and drought conditions occurring more often . <p> It is important to build better capability to simulate the day-to-day and intra-seasonal variability of monsoon in climate models with more confidence in projections . In the future , increasing population along with various developmental priorities will bring additional stresses on society and the environment , with serious implications for water resources , health and food security . <p> Thus , the possibility that the monsoon may become less stable as a result of climate change has serious consequences for India . <p> There is an urgent need to improve @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ measures will help millions to adapt to emerging scenarios and tide over the predicaments of climate change . Using state-of-the art climate models and observations , researchers are investigating the processes that control the monsoon rain and its variability and it is hoped that accurate scientific predictions about the unpredictable monsoon will be possible in the near future . <p> ( The author is senior programme officer with International Development Research Centre ( IDRC ) , New Delhi . This ability , called thermal acclimation , is necessary for insect survival over the cold winter months , but how this happens is still not well understood . <p> Since many insects carry disease , are crop pests or , on the positive side , are helpful to humans as pollinators , understanding the mechanisms behind thermal acclimation improves scientists ' ability to predict changes to insect populations as the Earth 's climate rapidly changes . <p> For the study , researchers raised common fruit flies , Drosophila melanogaster , from eggs through to their larval or maggot stages at room temperature ( 21 C ) . " We saw nearly a third of the fly 's genes increased or decreased in expression , and the abundance of roughly half of the metabolites changed at the same time , " said Brent Sinclair , Associate Professor at Western University and senior author of the study . Ultimately , this map will help drive us toward new applications in the realms of agriculture and disease transmission . "

@@9660883 <p> babble is rabble.ca 's discussion board but it 's much more than that : it 's an online community for folks who just wo n't shut up . It 's a place to tell each other -- and the world -- what 's up with our work and campaigns . <p> In a column on Tuesday , environmental blogger Robert Scribbler noted that the Northern Hemisphere Jet Stream had merged with the Southern Hemisphere Jet Stream . <p> " It 's the very picture of weather weirding due to climate change . Something that would absolutely not happen in a normal world , " he wrote . " Something , that if it continues , basically threatens seasonal integrity . " <p> " Like many extreme events resulting from human-forced climate change -- this co-mingling of upper level airs from one Hemisphere with another is pretty fracking strange , " Scribbler explained . " Historically , the Tropics -- which produce the tallest and thickest air mass in the world -- have served as a mostly impenetrable barrier to upper level winds moving from one Hemisphere to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ human-forced climate change , the Hemispherical Jet Streams have moved out of the Middle Latitudes more and more . " <p> " That 's bad news for seasonality , " he continued . " You get this weather-destabilizing and extreme weather generating mixing of seasons that is all part of a very difficult to deal with ' Death of Winter ' type scenario . " <p> Two bloggers have made a stunning claim that has spread like wildfire on the Internet : They say the Northern Hemisphere jet stream , the high-altitude river of winds that separates cold air from warm air , has done something new and outrageous . They say it has crossed the equator , joining the jet stream in the Southern Hemisphere . One said this signifies that the jet stream is ' wrecked ' , the other said it means we have a " global climate emergency . " <p> But these shrill claims have no validity -- air flow between the hemispheres occurs routinely . The claims are unsupported and unscientific , and they demonstrate the danger of wild assertions made by non-experts reaching and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ out to several atmospheric scientists , who have graduate degrees and are trusted sources in the profession , for their reaction to these claims . Without exception , they said air flow between the hemispheres is not at all uncommon . <p> " This is total nonsense , " said Cliff Mass , a professor of meteorology at the University of Washington . " Flow often crosses the equator . " <p> Mass added that the cross-equator flow identified by Scribbler and Beckwith is not between mid-latitude jet streams , as claimed . " The analysis is making mistakes that even one of my junior undergrads would not make , " Mass said . <p> Ryan Maue , a senior meteorologist with a doctoral degree who works at WeatherBell Analytics , agreed with Mass that the cross-equator flow is totally normal and not evidence of a joint hemispheric jet stream . " Cross-equatorial flow at both upper and lower levels is part of the seasonal transition of the Western Pacific monsoon through boreal summer , " he said . 
@@9664561 <h> Opinion Column <h> Terrorism : Is Canada ready ? <p> Prime Minister Justin Trudeau speaks to Canadian nuclear industry experts as he visits an nuclear industry expo taking place on the site of the Nuclear Security Summit in Washington , D.C. , on Friday , April 1 , 2016 . THE CANADIAN PRESS/Sean Kilpatrick <p> The Trudeau government continues to conduct a lengthy review of Canada 's defences and will supposedly produce a policy white paper in early 2017 . This is serious business and should not be taken lightly by either the governing Liberals or the Canadian people . <p> Why does defence policy matter ? A nation-state that can not defend its territory from foreign and/or domestic threats is not truly sovereign . And the first responsibility of the Canadian nation-state is to protect its citizens and ensure the security of the dominion . <p> The defence policy review must assess Canada 's obvious strategic vulnerabilities and determine the capabilities that the Canadian Armed Forces ( CAF ) will require to overcome those challenges . <p> For example , climate change will likely lead to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ clear challenge to Canadian sovereignty . How many and what type of naval vessels does Canada require to defend the North and assert effective control over Canadian territorial waters ? And does Canada require nuclear submarines to enhance Canadian control over the Arctic ? <p> In addition , how many modern fighter jets and long-range surveillance aircraft does Canada need to effectively assert control over this vast country ? <p> NATO <p> The defence policy review must examine Canada 's role in the North Atlantic Treaty Organization ( NATO ) and assess its strategic importance . The western alliance was established in 1949 to counter rising Soviet power in Europe . <p> As a charter member of NATO , Canada played a pivotal role in the alliance during the Cold War , stationing a significant force in western Europe to help deter a possible invasion by the Soviet Union . Although Canada 's commitment to the alliance waned in the 1970s under then prime minister Pierre Trudeau , this country has been and remains a respected member of NATO , which continues to be a source of international stability . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ invasions of Poland and other western allies . The prospect of a direct conflict with NATO discourages the Russian strongman from advancing beyond Ukraine in his campaign to expand Russia 's sphere of influence and restore its status as a global superpower . <p> It would be foolhardy for defence planners to seriously entertain the idea of withdrawing from NATO . Not only would a Canadian withdrawal harm the cohesiveness of the alliance and give Putin a propaganda victory , it would weaken Canada 's influence on the world stage . <p> Canada 's voice is heard in Europe precisely because it is committed to defending Europe . Were Canada to signal that it no longer cares about European security or stability , it is unlikely that the Europeans would care to hear what Ottawa has to say on any given issue . Canada would cease to matter in Europe . <p> NATO also serves as valuable multilateral counterweight to the Canada-U.S. defence alliance . While membership in NATO is optional , Canada can not disengage from the bilateral alliance . Canadian territory is inextricably linked to that of the United @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Canadians like it or not . <p> Without NATO , Canada would be isolated on strategic issues . And Ottawa would lack the support of former NATO allies and would thus be less capable of influencing America 's strategic priorities and plans . <p> NORAD <p> While NATO remains an important yet optional multilateral alliance , Canada must always actively participate in NORAD -- or risk losing its national sovereignty . <p> The North American Aerospace Defence Command agreement is the product of an official exchange of diplomatic notes between the Diefenbaker government and the Eisenhower administration in 1957 . The binational defence institution was formally established the following year , creating a series of continental radar stations to monitor North American airspace to warn of incursions by Soviet bombers . <p> Although Canada will always be the junior partner in the bilateral alliance , Canada nevertheless plays an important and vigorous role in NORAD , which helps to protect Canadian sovereignty by giving Ottawa a say in continental defence planning . <p> If Canada were to withdraw from NORAD , the United States would unilaterally defend North American airspace , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ NORAD enables Canada and the United States to effectively respond to occasional Russian incursions into North American airspace . And NORAD also gives Ottawa and Washington the capability to track and , if necessary , shoot down hijacked jetliners that pose a threat to civilian population centres , thereby averting a loss of life on the scale witnessed on Sept. 11 , 2001 , when jihadists attacked the United States . <p> Natural disasters <p> The massive wildfires that ravaged Fort McMurray and other Alberta communities in May demonstrated yet again the importance of the military in times of domestic crisis . And defence planners should take note of the role that CAF aircraft and helicopters played in efforts to assist first responders during the worst natural disaster in Canadian history . <p> Unfortunately , in its very first budget , the Trudeau government put $3.7 billion of planned military equipment spending on hold . To be clear , a defence policy review is useless if the Canadian military does not have the planes , helicopters , ships and advanced weaponry that it needs to protect Canada . <p> In times @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ first responders evacuate civilians , battle fires or build dikes . When reviewing defence policy , the Liberal government should not underestimate the importance of adequately funding military training programs , which give troops the skills and knowledge to jump into dangerous situations to help save lives and prevent mass destruction of homes and vital civilian infrastructure . <p> Were a major earthquake to strike British Columbia , civilian authorities and first responders would likely be overwhelmed by the scope of the catastrophe . And that 's when the military would be needed to step into the breach , airlifting life-saving supplies , clearing blocked roads and highways , searching for survivors , and maintaining law and order . <p> The defence review should carefully scrutinize current personnel levels in all branches of the CAF . For example , does the military have enough personnel to respond to multiple natural disasters in Canada while simultaneously meeting Canada 's overseas military commitments ? <p> Terrorism <p> The Trudeau government refuses to acknowledge that Canada is at war with a transnational jihadist movement that seeks to destroy liberal democracy , inflict mass civilian @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ To the government 's way of thinking , Canada can not be at war with the Islamic State , which controls territory in Iraq and Syria and has affiliates in Africa , because the terrorist caliphate is not a traditional nation-state . However , the Liberals ' definition of war is too narrow . <p> Defence planners need to recognize that the concept of war has become more elastic in the 21st century , an era in which religious and/or ethnic loyalty sometimes trump nationalism . <p> The Islamic State -- also known as ISIS , ISIL or Daesh -- is the best financed terrorist organization in history . Financed by the sale of oil exported from territories under its control and by the slave trade , the Islamic State can pay recruits , buy weapons , vehicles and other war material , giving the jihadist organization military capabilities superior to those of many small nation-states . That the U.S.-led coalition has yet to defeat ISIS demonstrates that the jihadists remain a powerful force . <p> Given that ISIS has directly threatened Canada , defence planners need to examine this country @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ terrorist onslaughts that rocked Paris and Brussels . <p> Well-financed terrorists can overwhelm civilian security forces and hold an entire city in terror for days . The siege of Mumbai by Islamic extremists in 2008 demonstrated that a major international city can be brought to its knees by a terrorist organization . <p> Could Canada cope with a Mumbai-style attack ? What would happen if ISIS attacked Toronto and Montreal simultaneously ? Could the Canadian Armed Forces quickly deploy to support local police and take the fight to the terrorists ? Defence planners need to answer these important questions .

@@9666432 <h> The world and our place in it have changed since the Pearson Report <p> In 1968 , the same year that CIDA was established , World Bank President Robert McNamara struck the Commission on International Development , chaired by former Canadian Prime Minister ( and Nobel Peace Prize winner ) Lester Pearson . <p> Although the Pearson Report contained many thoughtful points , the one that resonated the most was the call for rich countries to commit to devoting 0.7 per cent of their GDP to foreign aid by 1980 . Not surprisingly , Canada was an enthusiastic supporter of that target . In practice , the nearest Canada got to it was 0.55 per cent in 1975 . Official statements then and since have prevaricated about the aspiration but no government has been forthright enough to disown it . Canada 's foreign aid budget currently stands at about $4.4 billion ( 0.28 per cent of GDP ) . <p> Clearly , the dollar amount of the aid budget is only one measure among many . The Center for Global Development in Washington publishes a Commitment to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ a series of topics ( migration , trade , security , the environment , technology and finance ) in addition to the raw aid budget . Here too , Canada ranks in the middle of the pack . <p> The main high-level choice aid programs , including Canada 's , face is what share of the aid budget to allocate to multilateral organizations . Historically , a quarter to one third of Canada 's aid budget has been distributed through the multilateral channel . For a period in the 1980s and 1990s , debt forgiveness for developing countries in distress featured as an important component of foreign aid . In the past ten years , this has averaged about $100 million annually , and has been zero the past two years . But three other important choices remain to be made . <p> First , how to " focus " , or concentrate aid ? The past decade has seen a succession of discussions around " countries of focus " -- the twenty or so countries where the bulk of Canadian aid is concentrated , and where that concentration is meant @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ practice , given the small size of Canada 's aid budget , Canada is not the lead donor anywhere . <p> In the real world , it is hard to attribute development success to the activities of any single player ( and with success , it is guaranteed that many players will -- correctly -- rise to take the credit . ) In a world of spillover effects , concentrating on one country and not the neighbourhood makes no sense ( imagine how this might work if during the Ebola outbreak only one or two of Guinea , Sierra Leone and Liberia were part of Canada 's priorities . Thankfully for the champions of country focus , none were ) . <p> Time has a funny way of making seemingly diligent choices look foolish . The opposite : All three know that personal magnetism , and the trust and warmth it can build , is essential to harnessing the political capital needed for policy success @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , or the rise of Donald Trump , or the success of Philippines strongman Rodrigo Duterte -- or indeed the reasons so much of history is littered with people following leaders into sometimes bad decisions -- they need to remember that the intangibles of personality often override calculus and strategy . <p> The leaders of Britain 's " Remain " campaign appeared utterly bereft of any friendly aura . It hurt them against firebrand foes . Hillary Clinton also lacks it . This has hampered her quest to sell moderation against Trump , who is seductive to a large swathe of Americans . His opponents may see him as a thug ; to millions of Americans he is a plain-speaking , take-charge guy . <p> In his speech to the House of Commons , Obama said unoriginal things such as : " Canadians and Americans are united in our understanding that diversity is a source of strength . " And : " If a CEO makes more in a day than a typical employee makes in a year , that kind of inequality is not just bad for morale in the @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ economy . " And of course he urged us , while ( rightly ) flattering our armed forces , to do more for NATO . Nothing new in all this . But we lapped it up , soaking in the messages as fresh thinking for troubled times . <p> Of course , charisma , selfies , photo ops and sound bites have always underscored effective politics . They 're a challenge for strategists and pundits , but important signposts for voters . <p> So Trudeau used his Three Amigos charm offensive to focus mostly on tackling climate change . Obama used his to focus on security , and address extremism and insularity . Pe ? a Nieto wanted trade and access . Each spoke intelligently . And each knew a little charisma can go a very long way . <h> Comments <p> We encourage all readers to share their views on our articles and blog posts . @@9673237 <h> Climate Change Impacting Inland Fish <p> THUNDER BAY -- The impact of climate change is already having impacts on Northern Canada . Winter road seasons are shorter . One of the takeaway messages is that climate change effects on fish are rarely straightforward , and they affect warmwater and coldwater fish differently . <p> " Thanks to this synthesis , we can see the effects of climate change on inland fish are no longer just future speculation , but today 's facts , with real economic , social , and ecological impacts , " said Doug Austen , Executive Director of the American Fisheries Society and publisher of Fisheries magazine . Smallmouth bass , a popular recreational species , are expanding their range northward with climate change . This expansion can disrupt existing food webs but it also creates new prospects for recreational fishing . Because many recreational fishers want to catch smallmouth bass , managers may need new management techniques to accommodate the increased fishing demand while still maintaining the native coldwater fish communities . Consequently , said Paukert , the management process may likely be an exercise in managing expectations of the stakeholders for fisheries changing with climate change . <p> Other major findings : <p> Climate change may be altering abundance and growth of some North American inland fishes , particularly coldwater fish such as sockeye salmon , a species experiencing well-documented shifts in range , abundance , migration , growth , and reproduction . <p> Climate change may be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ together previously to hybridize . For example , in Canada , smallmouth bass have expanded their range , altering existing food chains because the species compete against other top predators for habitat and prey fish . <p> Droughts are forecasted to increase in frequency and severity in many parts of North America , especially in arid rivers . Such droughts exacerbate the impacts of water flow regulation in ways that affect people , fish , and aquatic systems . <p> " The current state of the science shows that climate change is impacting fish in lakes , rivers , and streams , but knowing that is just the first step in effectively addressing the changes to these important natural resources and the communities which depend upon them , " Lynch said . <p> The following papers are available in Fisheries @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Physiological basis of climate change impacts on North American inland fishes , authored by James E. @@9719765 <h> Carbon dioxide removal may be Prairies ' best hope <p> This week , our Three Amigos -- Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau , U.S. President Barack Obama , and Mexican President Enrique Pe ? a Nieto -- reiterated commitments to climate change mitigation and a greener energy sector with higher percentages of renewable energy . This is all commendable and predictable given Canadian , American and Mexican commitments to the Paris Climate Change Agreement to limit global warming to 1.5 degrees . <p> The more surprising outcome of the North American Leaders Summit was a commitment to accelerate research and development on clean technology projects such as " the capture of carbon dioxide for use as an industrial feedstock or for sequestration underground . " <p> Fred Chartrand / The Canadian Press <p> Mexican President Enrique Pe ? a Nieto , Prime Minister Justin Trudeau and U.S. President Barack Obama in Ottawa . <p> The implication is policymakers are quite seriously coming to terms with the technical challenge of achieving the Paris 1.5 C target , and the benefits of doing so -- all of which bears @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Prairies . <p> There is relatively little research that has looked specifically at the 1.5 C warming scenario , but there is some and what does exist shows a big advantage in achieving the Paris target . <p> Last year , a study by Erich Fischer of the Institute for Atmospheric and Climate Science in Zurich found the risk of very hot days increases significantly in the gap between 1.5 and 2 C. The likelihood of experiencing what was a once-in-a-thousand-days hot day has already increased fivefold . According to Fischer , the likelihood of such extremely hot weather doubles again at 1.5 C and doubles again if we go to 2 C. <p> The Prairie Climate Atlas tells the story well -- for Winnipeg , which currently experiences about 12 hot days a year ( above 30 C ) , by the latter decades of this century , that number could rise to more than 40 days a year , at which point we 'd have a climate resembling present-day north Texas . <p> The environmental and political logic of the Paris target is obvious -- it 's the technical @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ the story even more interesting . As of several weeks ago , the last holdout climate station in the world ( in Antarctica ) reported an atmospheric CO2 concentration above 400 parts per million ( ppm ) . Every station in the world is now reporting more than 400 ppm . <p> The current crop of global circulation models generally agrees that limiting warming to 1.5 C requires atmospheric CO2 to rise no further than 430 ppm , which means 300 billion tonnes of CO2 can be added to the atmosphere . However , even a very aggressive mitigation strategy that drops global CO2 emissions to zero by 2050 and stays at zero for the rest of the century produces 800 billion tonnes of additional CO2 . So , how do we resolve this rather fundamental 500-billion-tonne gap to achieve 1.5 degrees ? <p> According to Joeri Rogelj and his colleagues at the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis in Austria , the answer is simple and inescapable -- we use carbon dioxide removal ( CDR ) technology . It has existed on the fringes of climate science and policy for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ until recently ) , a distraction to the priority task of cutting CO2 emissions . That may have been true in 1980 or even 1990 , but Rogelj 's modelling shows we 've waited too long , and without CDR , no plausible pathway exists to limit warming to 1.5 C by 2100 . What were once rather outlandish ideas now have to be on the table -- the math does n't pencil out any other way . <p> So what is CDR ? As the name implies , it 's technology that removes CO2 from the atmosphere and ideally locks it up permanently . At its simplest it can be afforestation ( planting trees ) and managing agricultural soils to sequester more carbon in its organic matter . More complex approaches use energy to chemically strip CO2 molecules from ambient air to produce a pure CO2 stream for use in industrial applications or geological sequestration . <p> So what are the stakes for the Prairies ? We know the effects from climate change are amplified on the Prairies , and we 'll likely reap disproportionate benefit by limiting global warming @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to achieve 1.5 C have one thing in common -- they need productive geography to work , whether for afforestation , soil carbon sequestration or the renewable energy to power CDR . <p> And a lot of productive geography is one attribute the Canadian Prairies have in spades . @@9744055 <p> In 1978 , two geophysicists discovered a crater off the coast of the Yucatan Peninsula around the same time a scientific paper was released suggesting that a cataclysmic event was caused when a large asteroid slammed into Earth around 65 million years ago . Many scientists concluded that , after the collision , a massive cloud of super-heated dust and debris covered the globe , creating conditions that eventually wiped out the dinosaurs as they faced global cooling and the poisoning of food sources . <p> But not everyone was convinced . Some scientists believed that there was evidence to support a powerful volcanic eruption near Mumbai , India . <p> That theory has been hotly debated . Now a new study that reconstructed ocean temperatures in the Antarctic , supports the theory that both volcanism and climate change caused by the asteroid impact were responsible for causing the extinction of about 70 per cent of all species on Earth , including the dinosaurs . <p> Using new technology , the researchers studied 29 well-preserved mollusks that lived roughly 66 million years ago , found on Antarctica @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ about 7 C at that time , but two abrupt warming spikes were discovered . The first is believed to have been caused by the volcanic eruption in India ; the second after the asteroid slammed into Earth . <p> " We find that the end-Cretaceous mass extinction was caused by a combination of the volcanism and meteorite impact , delivering a theoretical ' one-two punch , ' " said Petersen , lead author of the study published on July 5 in the journal Nature Communications . <p> The temperatures in the Antarctic rose by about 8 C during the first warming event , likely as carbon dioxide became tapped in the atmosphere . The second , which was slightly smaller , occurred about 150,000 years later , around the time of impact . <p> Researchers believe that the warming likely created stress in the ecosystem , leaving them more vulnerable after the asteroid collision , thus causing the gradual extinction of the dinosaurs and most life on Earth .

@@9747358 <h> Divide and Conquer : The Threatened Community at the Heart of the PNW LNG Project <p> By Ash Kelly and Brielle Morgan for Discourse Media . For a full , interactive version of this investigative piece , visit Discourse Media . <p> For more than 5,000 years , First Nations people have collected plants and harvested red cedar on Lelu Island , which sits where the Skeena River meets the Pacific Ocean near Prince Rupert in northern British Columbia . Adjacent to some of the most critical salmon habitat on the West Coast , Lelu Island is considered so valuable that , according to local Indigenous oral histories , Indigenous tribes have long battled to control it . <p> Not much has changed today -- except that the battleground has shifted to Victoria and Ottawa . Prime Minister Justin Trudeau 's government is set to make a decision about Pacific NorthWest LNG ( PNWLNG ) ' s proposed $36-billion liquefied natural gas ( LNG ) project , which is majority-owned by the Malaysian energy company Petronas . Premier Christy Clark , who , already campaigning for re-election in May 2017 , has promised big on jobs and tax revenue she says LNG development will generate . She claims PNWLNG has wide backing among B.C. First Nations , whose support is critical . At a press conference on June 3 , Clark said , " It 's important that people in Vancouver and across the country see how much support there is for LNG in these communities . " <p> Last year , members of the Lax Kw'alaams First Nation , whose traditional territory includes Lelu Island , overwhelmingly rejected the proposed development on the island -- and almost $1.2 billion in promised benefits . Clark claims a breakthrough with Lax Kw'alaams occurred earlier this spring . Locals describe a community deeply divided over its future , desperate not to miss out on the economic opportunity LNG could provide , but with a majority opposed to developing Lelu Island . " Everybody 's bickering and fighting . @@9747919 <h> As the Arctic Ocean melts , the fishing talks begin <p> A small fishing boat sits at anchor off the hamlet of Pond Inlet , Nunavut Saturday August 23 , 2014 . ( Adrian Wyld/CP ) <p> Fishing in the central Arctic Ocean 20 years ago ? Impossible . Fishing in the central Arctic Ocean now ? Definitely possible , thanks to climate change . But if a meeting up in Iqaluit , Nunavut goes according to plan , there wo n't be any nets or rods in the icy waters until more research has been conducted . Starting Wednesday , delegations from ten nations , including the five Arctic coastal states -- Canada , Denmark ( Greenland ) , Russia , Norway and the U.S. -- are meeting to discuss the future of commercial fishing in the increasingly available international Arctic waters . <p> Trevor Taylor , the fisheries conservation director for the PEW Charitable Trusts ' Oceans North Canada , is attending the three-day meeting and says that so far , talks are going well . He spoke to Maclean 's about why coming to @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ and what we can expect when one is reached . <h> Q : Why are these ten nations meeting this week ? <p> A : I guess to go back in time , historically , for as long as humankind can remember , the central Arctic Ocean has been permanently covered in ice . And therefore , there 's been no ability for anybody to go in there and fish in any significant kind of way , unlike the situation in pretty well all of the rest of the oceans , including the southern ocean around Antarctica . Everybody has been , over the course of the past hundreds of years , and in some cases thousands , been able to go into these oceans and fish . <p> The central Arctic Ocean has n't afforded anybody that opportunity because it 's been covered with ice . And over the course of the last two decades in particular , ice cover has been receding and over the course of the last decades , more specifically , up to 40 per cent of the central Arctic Ocean , the international waters outside @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ , has been open water at the peak of the summer season . And that basically opens up a huge area where fishing fleets could , if they so desired , go in and explore for fishery resources , and if they found it , set up a fishery . The opportunity is becoming available . <h> Q : How is this meeting this year different from the meeting last summer ? <p> A : Last summer 's meeting was a meeting of the five Arctic Coastal states . That would be Russia , Norway , Denmark on behalf of Greenland , Canada , and the U.S.A. And those five have exclusive economic zones that ring the Arctic Ocean . They felt that there was a need to start to develop a consensus that unregulated fishing in the central Arctic Ocean should be prohibited , not just because of the impact on the central Arctic Ocean , but because some of these stocks , to the extent that they exist , could be transboundary stocks , could be migratory stocks , they could be straddling stocks that might have an impact @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ it was a non-binding agreement -- that they would not allow any of their fishing fleets to go into the international waters of the central Arctic Ocean to fish in advance of science being done , a management body established , and appropriate regulatory regime being put in place . <p> This one builds on that . So the five Arctic coastal states recognized that an international agreement needs more than the five Arctic coastal states , it needs the broader international community to be a party to the agreement and they recognize that the first place that they should go is to talk to the nations who have major fishing fleets . That would be Korea , China , Japan , the European Union , and Iceland . All those nations have huge fleets that travel around the world and would be probably some of the ones that would be most capable of going into the central Arctic Ocean given their past experience with international high seas fishing . The other thing I 'd say , the other caveat around that , is there 's no doubt in my mind and that of most people who are familiar with this issue , is that there will be an agreement regulating fishing in the international waters of Arctic . The question is whether it 'll be an agreement before fishing takes place , or whether it 's an agreement after fishing takes place . And our hope is that it 'll be an agreement prior to fishing taking place . <h> Q : And why is that ? <p> To use an overstated analogy , it 's easier to keep the horse in the barn than catch it after it gets out . It 's easier to find an agreement on something that you have n't had a dispute over @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ there 's nobody who can claim a historical attachment to any fishery resources in the central Arctic Ocean . Nobody has gone and overfished . It 's a level playing field right now . And that , I suspect , would make it easier to find an agreement . After fishing takes place , of course , then you get into a discussion not just about conservation and proper management , but of how shares get established . Who owns how much of the fish that is there or that might be there ? But the discussion now is very much around : How do you make sure that overfishing does n't take place ? How do you make sure the proper science is conducted ? How do you make sure that the ecosystem has what it needs to support itself before you take out a portion of the fish that are further down the food chain ? It allows for a discussion that is more about sustainability and proper management , than it is about how big your share of the catch should be . <h> Q : How do @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ Certainly from a Canadian perspective they do . @@9757387 <p> Call me an idealist , but I love nature 's many examples of sharing so that everyone wins . Scientists call this ' symbiosis ' - the sharing of resources between different organisms for the benefit of both . <p> As a long-time plant fanatic , I 'm fascinated by the ways that plants lure insects into helping them reproduce . The challenge for the plant is to entice something with legs or wings to bring them pollen from another plant so its eggs can become seeds . It 's a familiar story , played out by countless species of plants and animals - the very foundation of life renewing itself . <p> For the majority of plants , the solution is to offer a reward in the form of a sweet treat known as nectar . To advertise the location of this tasty treat , plants produce an amazing array of flowers of all shapes , sizes and colours . Scent is another lure , sometimes sweet and pleasant like the fragrant lilacs that attract foraging butterflies . Sometimes the scent is not so pleasant - @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ on the ground and emit a mild odour of rotting meat . This attracts ground-dwelling beetles , which scuttle into the flowers to investigate , while carrying pollen from one flower to another . <p> For their services in helping plants produce seeds , insects receive tasty nectar , rich in carbohydrates , as well as a surplus of protein-rich pollen which is a staple food for many pollinating insects . All the players benefit in the dance of pollination . <p> Who Are the Pollinators ? <p> Many insects , and a few birds and mammals , can help pollinate plants . Bees , wasps , flies , butterflies , beetles and moths can all carry pollen from one flower to another . But the star of the show is the bee family . Bees have hairy bodies with uniquely branched hairs - perfect for pollen to ' stick ' and be transported , sometimes over long distances . No other insect can rival bees for their ability to transport pollen . <p> Most of us are familiar with honeybees - originally from Europe and Asia , but few people @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ bees native to Ontario . While they come in a great variety of shapes and sizes , they all share the branched hairs that make them excellent pollen transporters . <p> Many native bees live solitary lives , and some only live as adults for a few weeks of the year . Their life cycle coincides with the bloom period of their favourite plants . They mate and lay their eggs in hollow plant stems , in burrows in the ground , or in small holes in wood , to complete their life cycle and emerge again next year . These solitary bees do n't have a colony to defend , so they 're not aggressive , and rarely sting . <p> Bumblebees are unusual among native bees , in that they live in colonies , usually underground . Mated queens are the only ones to survive the winter , ready to start a new colony next year . Bumblebees can sting , but only if provoked or if their hive is threatened . <p> What is the problem ? <p> The dramatic decline in bee populations worldwide has received much @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ diseases and pests , climate change , as well as pesticides such as neonicotinoids are all contributors to this worrying population crash . The most immediate impact on people is the threat to our food spply . An estimated 1/3 of human food relies on insect pollination , including all fruits , and vegetables such as beans , peas , cucumbers and squash . <p> A more insidious result is the potential impact on plants which depend on bees for reproduction . Plants are the foundation of ecology - passing their bounty of food along the food chain to all living things . When plant species are lost , so are the myriad life forms that depend on them . Biodiversity is the hallmark of healthy , stable ecosystems . All threats to biodiversity require serious attention and action . <p> What can be done ? <p> Addressing the decline in pollinator populations requires cooperative action from many sectors . Excellent programs are emerging to raise awareness of the importance of pollinators in general , and bees in particular . ' Farms at Work ' have spearheaded many rural education programs @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ 's Guide to Conserving Native Pollinators in Ontario ' , reinforcing the importance of fencerows and an abundance of wild plants to provide all-season food and shelter for bees . Environmental education centres such as Camp Kawartha teach children the importance of bees in local ecology , and Otonabee Conservation works with schools and other community groups to plant pollinator-friendly gardens . Citizen groups such as Peterborough Pollinators are working to establish a network of pollinator-friendly gardens . <p> Homeowners can provide havens for pollinators in their own yards , by understanding a few basic principles . <p> Urban gardens and greenspaces <p> There is no one magic ' bee plant ' that will support the wide variety of bee species living in our area . Bees have evolved in many shapes and sizes , with a diversity of mouth structures , each dependent on specific flower shapes to access the nectar and pollen within . As in nature , diversity is the key in selecting an array of bee-friendly plants . <p> Most plants have a specific bloom period , which lasts for a few weeks each year . It @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ times , so there is an ongoing food source for pollinators . This year , the early warm weather brought young queen bumblebees out early . They found sustenance in early bulbs such as hyacinth and early blooming trees and shrubs such as willows , serviceberry and red elderberry . In May , fruit trees such as apples support a wide variety of bee species , as do early blooming perennials such as dwarf catmint , and wild plants such as wild mustard and dandelion . Strawberry blossoms and lilacs are also May staples for pollinators . <p> In June , ornamental alliums and chive blossoms are loved by many small native bees , and raspberry blossoms , penstemon and shrub roses are popular with bees as well . Summer favourites include black-eyed Susan , purple coneflower , blazing star , globe thistle and bee balm , as well as milkweeds and herbs such as oregano , thyme and mints . Late bloomers such as goldenrod and asters provide food in the fall for bees , and important sustenance for the migrating Monarch butterfly . <p> Gardeners should be aware that @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hybrids that do n't produce nectar or pollen . When plants are bred for extra-large flowers , new colours or extended bloom periods , the ability to produce seed is sometimes lost , and the bees lose a food source as a result . <p> In general , plants with an abundance of small flowers are more bee-friendly than large showy blooms . Native and heirloom plants are a great place to start . Experimenting with a variety of flowers , and watching how pollinators react , adds a whole new dimension of challenge and wonder to the gardening process , and a great feeling of satisfaction in knowing that you 're helping to boost species in decline . <p> Gardeners can also help to provide habitat for solitary bees by leaving areas of garden soil undisturbed and unmulched . Many tiny native bees lay their eggs in bare soil , and when gardens are heavily mulched , these bees ca n't get through . Try sinking some small flowerpots filled with sand in the garden and leave them undisturbed as a nesting site for ground-nesting native bees . These bees @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ they are not defending a colony . <p> Unmown areas of greenspace on public and private land can also provide a haven for pollinators . However , given the abundance of invasive exotic plants in many urban areas , ongoing observation and management of unmown spaces will be necessary to prevent further spread of undesirable plants such as garlic mustard and dog strangling vine . Floral displays in public gardens can be selected to help support pollinators as well as providing colourful beauty . <p> Be a bee watcher <p> It 's incredibly satisfying to watch nature respond to your efforts to attract new life into your yard , and to sharpen your senses and ability to recognize many different plants and pollinators . ' Bumblebee Watch " is a program to help novices learn to identify various species of bumblebees , and to track their status in North America . You can send a photograph of any bumblebee to the program , and their experts will confirm an identification . It 's a great way to compile your own photo gallery of pollinators , and to learn which local plants @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ information , visit their website at www.BumbleBeeWatch.org <p> Cathy Dueck is one of the local naturalists filling in for regular columnist Drew Monkman , who is on a summer break .

@@9778344 <p> Editor 's note : This report was first published by Yale Environment 360 in October 2015 , and is republished with kind permission . <p> The boreal forest wraps around the globe at the top of the Northern Hemisphere in North America and Eurasia . Also known as taiga or snow forest , this landscape is characterized by its long , cold and snowy winters . In North America it extends from the Arctic Circle of northern Canada and Alaska down into the very northern tip of the United States in Idaho , Washington , Montana , and Minnesota . It 's the planet 's single largest biome and makes up 30 per cent of the globe 's forest cover . <p> Moose are the largest ungulate in the boreal , adapted with their long legs to wade in its abundant marshes , lakes , and rivers eating willows , aspen and other plants . In the southern boreal forest of northern Minnesota , moose were once plentiful , but their population has plummeted . Thirty years ago , in the northwest part of the state , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ hundred . In the northeast part , they have dropped from almost 9,000 to 4,300 . They 've fallen so far , so fast that some groups want them listed as endangered in the Midwest . <p> The boreal forest extends around the earth at the top of the Northern Hemisphere . Moose carcasses deteriorate rapidly before they are found , and so forensics has not been able to determine why they are dying . Some experts surmise it could be that tens of thousands of ticks that mob an animal and weaken it . Others think it 's a parasite called liver flukes , or the fact that winters have gotten so warm the animals ca n't regulate their body temperature and die from heat stress . <p> But Dennis Murray , a professor of ecology at Trent University in Peterborough , Ontario , thinks the dying moose of Minnesota and New Hampshire and elsewhere are one symptom of something far bigger -- a giant forest ecosystem that is rapidly shrinking , dying , and otherwise changing . " The boreal forest is breaking apart , " he says . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ <p> Many scientists , in fact , are deeply concerned about the state of the world 's largest forest . The Arctic and the boreal region are warming twice as fast as other parts of the world . Permafrost is thawing and even burning , fires are burning unprecedented acres of forest , and insect outbreaks have gobbled up increasing numbers of trees . Climate zones are moving north 10 times faster than forests can migrate . And this comes on top of increased industrial development of the boreal , from logging to oil and gas . The same phenomena are seen in Russia , Scandanavia , and Finland . <p> The boreal forest extends around the earth at the top of the Northern Hemisphere . Photo : Hare and Ritchie , 1972 . <p> These disturbing signals of a forest in steep decline are why NASA just launched a large-scale research project called ABoVE -- Arctic Boreal Vulnerability Experiment , a " major field campaign " with 21 field projects over the next decade . But the studies will confirm in detail what many know is well underway . <p> @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ point this century , " said Anatoly Shvidenko , of the International Institute for Applied Systems Analysis and a co-author of a survey of a recent research on boreal forests in the journal Science . " It is urgent we place more focus on climate mitigation and adaptation with respect to these forests . " <p> A tipping point would include the mother of all concerns : the unbridled melting of permafrost , one of the main thrusts of the ABoVE project . The permafrost in the boreal is more susceptible to thawing than in the Arctic because it 's closer to the freezing point . If large-scale melting occurs it would release more carbon dioxide and methane , which have been bound up in the frozen soil for thousands of years , and bring on more warming , and then more thawing , a dangerous loop . " Scientists call it a positive feedback , but most people call that a vicious cycle , " said Peter Griffith , chief support scientist for the ABoVE project . <p> Murray has been researching the boreal forest for 25 years , and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ In British Columbia , 80 per cent of the province 's mature lodgepole , another boreal species , have recently died from the mountain pine beetle , whose range and season both expanded greatly because of a warmer world . White and black spruce , the main trees species in the boreal , are also dying in vast numbers " The southwest Yukon looks dramatically different than it did 25 years ago when I did my master 's degree , " he said . " Everywhere you go there is deadfall . " <p> NASA has also seen a lot of forest browning in its studies , large swaths of forests with reduced growth that turn brown in the hotter than normal summers , and which contribute to much bigger and hotter fires and the thawing of the permafrost . " Severe fires burn a foot or more of organic soil and that 's the insulating layer that keeps the permafrost frozen , " said Scott Goetz , lead scientist on the ABoVE project . " Once that is removed the thaw is much more rapid . " <p> The fires @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ organic soil you get deciduous re-growth that lasts for decades , " said Goetz . " Maybe it will never come back as coniferous . " <p> Typically , when black spruce dies , it is replaced with new black spruce . " That 's been going on for a long , long time , but not anymore , " Murray says . " You lose spruce and you lose everything that lives in spruce and that is basically everything in the boreal forest . We 're seeing the same phenomena that we 've seen with moose with lynx and snowshoe hares . And caribou are going belly up very , very fast . Their ranges are receding northward rapidly . " <p> The boreal is also home to some five billion birds . Many species have shifted their ranges north . " Climate change is having an impact much more quickly than we thought , " said Jeff Wells , a senior scientist with the International Boreal Campaign who focuses on birds . " Shifts that researchers thought would take place over 50 or a hundred years have taken place @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ such a large system are complex . The forest is n't merely receding north , it 's dying in some places in its interior and surviving quite well in others . A 2015 study found that while boreal spruce forest in interior Alaska is dying out because of warm temperatures , the same forest on the state 's west coast is thriving . <p> The dying spruce and moose and lynx and other changes are the dots that scientists are trying to connect to get a sense of what the boreal forest in North America will look like in the next half century . <p> The caveat is that in a system this massive and complex there are so many variables it 's difficult to forecast with much certainty . The projected changes , for example , are based on the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change 's temperature forecast of a rise of some 10 degrees by 2100 . Should things warm faster or go higher , the changes could come faster and be deeper or different than modeled . And many changes could simply be unpredictable . <p> Murray 's @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ boreal in Ontario and Quebec , a gap some 500 by 350 kilometres . It will essentially split the contiguous forest into two separate forests -- one to the east , the other to the west -- as the black spruce and white spruce disappear . That gap could then become grassland or Carolinian , the forest ecosystem that dominates south of the boreal in Ontario , characterized by oak , maple , black walnut and other deciduous species . <p> As the spruce goes , so goes its inhabitants . " We 're predicting there 's going to be no lynx , moose , or hare in central Ontario in the years to come , " Murray says , " so we 're going to have disjunct populations on either side . " It could cause a break between populations of species and a loss of genetic diversity . <p> Murray has coined a term for the patchy quality of the effects of warming on the boreal -- climate fragmentation . " Because it 's a gradual transition , it wo n't be real boreal and it wo n't be @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ likely be less stable and more open to invasives . " <p> Changes in snow cover are already driving changes . In some places snow covers the ground for shorter periods , and the conditions of the snow are also changing . Instead of three feet of fluffy snow all winter , temperatures rise and melt the snow and then get cold and freeze it and compact it into ice , again and again . In such conditions , lynx , which have thick , padded paws that serve as de facto snowshoes and allow them to hunt atop deep snow , loses it evolutionary advantage . " It affects their ability to survive , " says Murray . " Coyotes , on the other hand , are extremely plastic and flexible . They were n't in the boreal a hundred years ago , but they are there now . They are n't everywhere , because they do n't do well in deep snow , but that 's changing . " They are competing with lynx by foraging for their kills and preying on hares and squirrels . <p> The die-off @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ unpredictable repercussions on the global climate system . When British Columbia 's lodgepole forests died , the province went from being a carbon sink to a carbon source because the dead forests released massive amounts of stored CO2 . If the spruce forests of the boreal disappear they could also alter climate systems by releasing CO2 . Because they are dark , they also absorb heat , but a treeless , snow-covered landscape would reflect far more solar energy back into the atmosphere . <p> White spruce , shown above near the Denali Highway in Alaska , have been dying off in the boreal forest . Photo : NOAA . <p> Knowing what could happen in the next 50 or 60 years , and where , is important for conservation and other strategies . The boreal , especially in Canada , is n't just a forest . Hundreds of First Nations call the boreal home , and they depend on it for sustenance , hunting moose and caribou , picking berries , and fishing . Paper and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ The research NASA is doing will be used to help determine how communities and land managers in the boreal might adapt to changes . @@9788425 <h> Knowledge of currents enables frigate birds ' amazing endurance <p> Europeans named the birds " frigate " for their resemblance to the swift warships . They look powerful , with their forked tails and long , slender wings ; the shadows they cast on the sea surface could just as easily belong to a flock of pterodactyls . They make incredible feats of endurance -- flying for two months without once setting foot on land , for instance -- seem almost effortless : they ascend to altitudes of 2,000 feet and drop back down to sea level again with just a single flap of their wings . <p> " It is impressive , " said Henri Weimerskirch , an ornithologist at the National Centre for Scientific Research in France . " There is no other bird species like them . " <p> Weimerskirch would know -- he spent two years tracking 80 frigate birds to understand their behaviour , which seems to defy all laws of gravity and biology . Though they feed exclusively on fish , the creatures can not swim . Instead they fly for @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ tropics in search of food that swims close enough to the surface for them to snatch it out of the water . <p> They 're able to do this , Weimerskirch reported last week in the journal Science , because of an incredible , intuitive mastery of air currents . Combining data from GPS trackers , heart-rate monitors and accelerometers affixed to the birds with local weather reports , he and his colleagues figured out how frigate birds take advantage of thermals and trade winds to fly over vast distances for long periods of time -- all without expending much more energy than they would sitting in a nest . <p> Frigate birds are the only seabirds that lack waterproof feathers -- if they dive into the ocean or even land on its surface , the water will soak their plumage and prevent them from taking flight again . This should be a death knell to a species that dines exclusively on fish , but it 's not . Frigate birds can soar high above the ocean , eyes peeled for movement in the water below -- a sign a large @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fish to the surface . <p> " When it sees its prey , it flies down head foremost to the water 's edge , very swiftly takes its prey out of the sea with his bill and immediately mounts again as swiftly ; never touching the water with his bill , " a 17th-century observer wrote . <p> " It 's a very , very specific niche and way of attacking prey , " said Weimerskirch . " But the prey are very patchy ... it takes days and days to encounter one opportunity . So they have to cover very long distances to find it . " <p> That 's where the birds ' soaring abilities come in . Their large , lightweight wings ( their wing **25;32;TOOLONG ratio is higher than any other bird 's ) allow them to take advantage of the slightest breezes . They soar upward on thermals , much the way hang-gliders do , and then glide back down gradually over the course of many kilometres . Unlike gliders , they also take advantage of the air currents within clouds to rise even higher when @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ ascend as fast as four to five metres per second . Few other birds and even most planes would n't attempt this because of the potential for turbulence . <p> The birds also know to avoid the " doldrums , " equatorial regions of the Atlantic and Pacific where light , capricious winds , unpredictable calms and sudden storms could spell doom for ancient mariners and modern birds . <p> Allowing air currents to do the work of lifting them makes frigate birds ' flight hugely efficient . The heart-rate monitors Weimerskirch and his colleagues attached to the birds showed they did n't flap their wings at all while gaining altitude -- the energy costs of ascending thousands of feet in the air were the same as when they were sitting still . <p> And that , in turn , allowed them to travel vast distances over unimaginable periods of time . An adult bird can fly continuously for more than a month , covering 400 kilometres per day , without stopping once . Some crossed the Indian Ocean several times without setting a single foot on land . <p> It @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ epic journeys . Weimerskirch said there 's evidence they can shut down half their brains as they ascend on updrafts . <p> " They are probably getting small bouts of sleep at this time -- maybe two to three minutes , " he said . A subsequent study with miniature loggers that monitor sleep will test this hypothesis . <p> Juvenile birds were especially strong endurance fliers -- likely because they are going through a " dispersal phase , " in which they journey as far as possible from their home nests , like 18-year-olds who insist they must fly to the other side of the country to go to college . One juvenile stayed aloft for more than two months . Another flew nearly 56,000 kilometres ( a distance greater than the circumference of the Earth ) in 185 days . On only four of those days did it land on an island to rest , and even then , only for a few hours . <p> But these birds owe a lot to their parents , who spend more time teaching their young the ways of the world than @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ eight months flying with their parents before setting out on their own . <p> " That 's a very long period , " said Weimerskirch . " And it 's probably because it 's complicated to learn how to fly . It takes time to learn to deal with all the conditions and all the constraints they have . " <p> " When you see the flight pattern of a frigate bird , " he added , " you understand . " <p> But scientists are worried about how climate change might affect frigate birds ' flight ; shifting weather patterns could disrupt the flight techniques frigate birds spend so long learning . Warming oceans will likely become less productive , and the infrequent appearances of food that frigate birds depend on may disappear . <p> You can comment on most stories on winnipegfreepress.com . You can also agree or disagree with other comments . All you need to do is be a Winnipeg Free Press print or e-edition subscriber to join the conversation and give your feedback .
