@@9929141 <h> The future of hydro in a warming world <p> People have harnessed energy from moving water for thousands of years . Greeks used various types of water wheels to grind grain in mills more than 2,000 years ago . In the late 1800s , people figured out how to harness the power to produce electricity . Throughout the 20th century and into the 21st , hydropower has expanded , producing about 17 per cent of the world 's electricity by 2014 and about 85 per cent of renewable energy -- and it shows no signs of slowing . <p> According to the online magazine WaterWorld , " An expected 3,700 major dams may more than double the total electricity capacity of hydropower to 1,700 GW within the next two decades , " -- including in my home province of B.C. , where the government has started a third dam on the Peace River at Site C. " Hydropower is the most important and widely-used renewable source of energy , " the U.S. Geological Survey says . <p> But how " green " is hydropower , and how @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ fluctuations and shortages ? To some extent , it depends on the type of facility . <p> The Center for Climate and Energy Solutions notes some large dams are used mainly for water storage or flood control with power generation an additional function , while some are used primarily to generate electricity . Small hydro such as run-of-river is installed on running water and does n't use water stored in reservoirs . Pumped storage facilities do n't generate additional energy , but store energy by pumping water from a lower reservoir to a higher one when demand and price are low , sometimes using renewable energy , and release water through turbines when price and demand are high . All have varying environmental impacts . <p> One of the biggest trade-offs with large-scale hydro facilities is that building them often means flooding land used for farming and human communities . Damming rivers also impedes fish -- even with technologies like fish ladders -- and can harm wildlife habitat and alter river temperatures , dissolved oxygen levels and flows . And while hydropower creates fewer pollution and climate problems than fossil fuel @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to build a dam and flood land can release greenhouse gases . And as vegetation decays and water levels fluctuate , methane -- a greenhouse gas far more potent than carbon dioxide -- can build up and escape from reservoirs . <p> Ironically , although hydropower is seen as an energy source that helps slow global warming , in many areas its viability is threatened by climate change . Rising greenhouse gas emissions and a warming world affect the entire hydrological cycle -- surface and ground water , glaciers , precipitation , runoff and evaporation . Shifting precipitation patterns and increased droughts are changing water levels in rivers and behind hydro dams . <p> The massive Hoover Dam on the Colorado River is operating at 30 per cent capacity , and new turbines have to be installed at lower elevation because of low precipitation and drought . In Nepal , " low water levels rendered a brand-new dam project ineffective and cut off the water supply farther downstream , " said John Matthews , director of fresh water and adaptation at Conservation International , in Scientific American . <p> Matthews and @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ that climate change puts 40 per cent of hydro development investments at risk . They recommend an approach to dams and hydro that takes climate change into account , by building projects in stages so adjustments can be made as more is known about climate patterns , or by " building with nature " rather than on top of it . <p> Meanwhile , as more environmentally benign power technologies become increasingly cost-effective and viable , the U.S. is removing older dams , many of which do n't have fish ladders , because costs to maintain and repair them are too high , as are environmental impacts . <p> Hydropower will remain part of the clean-energy equation , but we need to find the least disruptive , most efficient methods . Scientist Peter Gleick , president and cofounder of California 's Pacific Institute , says the key to supplying energy to growing populations in a warming world will be to use a diversity of power sources . @@9967719 <h> Prime Minister 's Youth Council Backgrounder <p> Ottawa , Ontario <p> 19 July 2016 <p> The Government of Canada is committed to listening to the issues that matter most to young people . Canadians , aged 16 to 24 , will provide the Prime Minister with non-partisan advice on national issues such as employment , access to education , building stronger communities as well as climate change and clean growth , among others . <p> About the Prime Minister 's Youth Council <p> Up to 30 Council members will be selected . These members will come from diverse communities from all regions of Canada , in order to bring a range of knowledge and experience to the table . They will sit on the Council for a mandate of up to two years , and will be compensated for their time while conducting Youth Council business . <p> Council members will meet both online and offline @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ to them , their community , and their country . They will interact with each other outside of meetings to discuss ideas and upcoming activities , and will engage with their communities . They will meet with the Prime Minister up to four times a year . <p> Applying to Become a Council Member <p> Applicants will be asked to fill out an online form in which they must provide background information on themselves , their community involvement , and ideas for Canadian youth . <p> Selections for the Youth Council will be made in two intervals . The first wave of Youth Council members will meet with the Prime Minister in the fall , while members selected during the second wave will join the second meeting in 2017 . <p> The selection process will be conducted in two stages . In the first phase , a pool of approximately 300 youth will be chosen from the entire pool of applicants . In this phase , we will create three pools of approximately 100 candidates each who will be invited to the second stage of the selection process . The first @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ highest scores in community engagement in each region of Canada . This will ensure that there are candidates who have a strong context of the issues and activities of their communities , so are best to represent their constituents . The second pool will consist of 100 randomly selected candidates . This will allow for a fair and broad representation of all youth applicants . The final pool of 100 candidates will be formed based on diversity indicators , to allow the large pool of 300 to be fully representative of the diversity of Canada . <p> The second stage of the selection process will invite the top 300 applicants to conduct a video interview and submit their resumes to a secure online platform and give their ideas for Canadian youth . This additional information will be used to select the top candidates for the Youth Council . <p> Youth Engagement <p> The application will have an option for youth to not apply for the Youth Council , but have their information submitted to a database for further youth engagement opportunities . This database will be shared with other federal departments @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ applicants of the Youth Council will also have their information submitted to this database . All applicants must click ' agree ' to the sharing of their information on the application , prior to submitting . <p> We are thrilled to be partnering with you in this work and look forward to finding innovative ways to spread the word , once the call has been officially launched .

@@9976938 <p> Bill 6 is the farm safety legislation . It provides for compensation for farm workers injured on the job and gives them the right to refuse unsafe work . Before the enactment of Bill 6 , Alberta was the only Canadian province that did not legislate these rights for farm employees . Farmers and ranchers in those other jurisdictions seem to be coping . Thanks to the NDP , Alberta finally entered the 21st century . <p> The numbers the member relates regarding the carbon tax are from a preliminary government analysis done in November 2015 , which assumed about half of the money raised by the carbon tax would go directly to general government revenues . @@9978770 <h> Global Affairs ' women 's champion outward bound to Sydney <p> Chief of Protocol Angela Bogdan and Govenor General David Johnston welcome U.S. President Barack Obama to Ottawa June 29 , 2016 for the North American Leaders ' Summit . Ms. Bogdan is to the right of the GG , in red . ( Contributed photo ) <p> After more than 30 years as a professional diplomat , the past three as Canada 's chief of protocol , Angela Bogdan spent some time with iPolitics recently looking back on her career before she heads to another posting as consul general in Sydney , Australia . <p> Bogdan did n't grow up hankering for a life in the sometimes stuffy , occasionally physically and verbally perilous but always fascinating diplomatic corps . <p> She recalls how , more than 30 years ago , she had actually doubted her chances at a career in the field . <p> After high school , Bogdan , then 18 , went to Seneca College to train in cosmetology and fashion retailing . This led her , briefly , to advertising , which @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . <p> In her early twenties , she went back to school , earning a combined Bachelor of Arts/Bachelor of Education from York University . <p> She did so while raising her son , Jason , alone . <p> With a B.Ed. , Bogdan says she thought she would become a teacher . However , those plans changed after she started her master 's , also at York . <p> Pursuing a degree in strategic studies ( a subject she compares to nuclear and defence policy ) , Bogdan recalls being " really inspired " by professor Rod Byers and his course , War and Peace in the Nuclear Age . <p> " I was really excited about wanting to be part of making the world a safer place , " she says , adding , " I know that sounds a little corny . " <p> It was Byers , director of the Strategic Studies program , who suggested Bogdan pursue a career in diplomacy . She can still remember him walking down a hallway at York , with an advertisement for the Foreign Service exam . <p> Initially , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ she says she told Byers , " ' They 're never going to hire me . I 'm a single mother . This is the diplomatic corps . ' " <p> His response , Bogdan says , was : " I think you 'd be fantastic at this . " <p> Bogdan wrote the exam , but remained skeptical -- even after she received a call for an interview . <p> The interviewers , she said , did ask about her transition from cosmetology and fashion retailing to strategic studies . But they hired her . <p> " Nobody was more shocked than I was that I actually got in , " she says . <p> Bogdan joined the Defence Relations Division of the former Department of External Affairs in 1984 as a peacekeeping desk officer responsible for Canadian operations in Cyprus . <p> That launched a career whose high points have included postings as high commissioner to Sri Lanka and the Maldives , ambassador to the former Federal Republic of Yugoslavia , political counsellor in Warsaw , deputy political advisor at Canada 's Mission to NATO and vice consul in @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of protocol in 2013 , following a stint of a similar length as inspector general . <p> In her current role , Bogdan leads the Office of Protocol within the recently rebranded Department of Global Affairs . <p> The job is not , as some might gather from the title , about place settings , curtsies and the elaborate arcana of exchanging business cards in Japan . <p> Broadly speaking , the office is responsible for state protocol , which , Bogdan says , " is all about projecting Canada to the world . " <p> On the one hand , Bogdan and her team have to " take care " of the diplomatic corps , the roughly 8,000 diplomats posted in or accredited to Canada . This involves providing them with a host of support services and , in large part , handling their outreach . <p> " We 're resourced and mandated to provide opportunities for them to get outside of the Ottawa bubble and experience Canada in all of its manifestations , " Bogdan says . <p> Most recently , for example , the office organized an " @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ of diplomatic mission . Bogdan 's team played a key role in hosting the summit , co-ordinating , among other things , security , hospitality and media relations . <p> The same is true for out-of-state events , such as Prime Minister Justin Trudeau 's official visit to Washington , D.C. , earlier this year . Praising the White House for planning an " extremely effective " visit , Bogdan says that her role at the event included circulating during the state lunch and dinner to check in on the other Canadian delegates . <p> One @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ trip took place during the opening ceremonies on the South Lawn of the White House . @@9978773 <h> With natural capital and trust , Canada can become an agrifood powerhouse Add to ... <p> Ted Bilyea is chair and David McInnes is president and CEO of the Canadian Agri-Food Policy Institute . <p> Ted Bilyea is chair and David McInnes is president and CEO of the Canadian Agri-Food Policy Institute . <p> What would you guess is the single most important ingredient in modern food production ? Good seeds ? Rainfall ? Fertilizer ? The surprising answer is that around the world , the scarcest and most precious resource for producing food is trust . Luckily , Canada has natural advantages that could allow the people of the world to view us as their most trusted food source -- if we make smart decisions . <p> To this point , much of the conversation about global food production has revolved around quantity : How will we produce enough for billions more people ? But this is not the toughest challenge . <p> The bigger question is n't whether we can produce enough food but whether we can do so sustainably , without bankrupting the planet @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ : our water , soil and the biodiversity of living organisms . <p> Around the world , trust in food production is taking a beating as the depletion of natural capital continues . In many areas , water use -- especially agricultural water use -- is exceeding natural recharge rates . Algae blooms , fostered by the overuse of fertilizer and the runoff of phosphorus from towns and cities , are threatening oceans and lakes . In Europe and elsewhere , pesticide levels in groundwater are a concern . In China , people have come to distrust local food production so much that there is a booming trade in online imported food . People are also becoming concerned about the links between health and food production . <p> Although most are not aware of the science behind these issues , consumers everywhere are growing increasingly uneasy about how the food they eat is produced . This concern peeks through in popular movements about GMO foods , organic produce , " buy local " and so forth . But these are only stalking horses for the more serious problems . <p> Winning @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ we grow food . Agriculture needs to show how it lives within the world 's limited natural capital and actually enhance it . For instance , the global agriculture sector can shift from just improving its own carbon emissions to soaking up a substantial portion of emissions from fossil fuel greenhouse gases ( GHG ) . Evidence suggests that as the price of carbon rises , properly managed soils might make this eventually possible . Canada needs to be bold in advancing such innovative thinking . <p> Many countries are going to struggle with rising costs of food production as their environmental burdens increase . Countries that seriously deplete their aquifers are facing water deficits . Others have cleared vast tracts of tropical forests -- the great carbon sinks -- for agricultural use . They have been facing consumer boycotts and sanctions as they become substantial GHG emitters and destroyers of ecosystems . <p> Supply chains are responding . For example , Canada is taking a leading role in sustainable beef production . Our retailers are part of a global effort to source seafood sustainably . Many producers here and abroad @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ companies are improving energy and water use . <p> Our strategic opportunity is recognizing that many countries will find it challenging to preserve , let alone enhance , natural capital . Canada , on the other hand , possesses an abundance of renewable freshwater and arable land relative to its population . Even our dreaded winters provide an agricultural advantage , acting as a natural pesticide . <p> Canada can define a powerful food brand as more and more consumers seek out trusted and more responsible suppliers . This is what the Canadian Agri-Food Policy Institute calls Canada 's " big possibility . " Canada can position itself as a preferred food source and derive economic benefits from doing so . <p> But are we doing enough to truly leverage Canada 's potential ? We lack a common goal . We can aim to produce more food , to do so sustainably and to improve its nutritional quality -- all at the same time . This would place Canada even further at the leading edge of global food innovation . This effort will require strong collaboration across the food system , @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ . It also extends to scientists , technology providers , financial institutions , the health community and others . <p> There would obviously be an important role for government . In Calgary this week , federal , provincial and territorial agriculture ministers will be discussing the issue of trust from the standpoint of maintaining the agrifood sector 's social licence to operate . Tackling the big issues confronting the sector ( such as climate change ) also requires a more co-ordinated Canadian science agenda . Carbon pricing will change behaviour , drive innovation and allow markets to properly allocate resources . National data and measures can track our progress . These steps will help deepen trust . <p> But we must be smart about how we impose new regulations . We want to lead without giving our competitors a significant cost advantage . With its natural capital assets , Canada has a chance to improve its competitiveness if it can encourage consumers here and abroad to increasingly value natural capital and better reflect food 's real ecological cost . <p> The expectations of consumers , our customers and even investors are @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ transformation in the way we look at food and the natural capital behind it . By coming together as a nation , we can build Canadian agriculture and food into an even greater economic powerhouse . <h> Restrictions <p> All rights reserved . @@9982339 <p> Energy required by data centers is on constant rise which represents a challenge for the climate change . RoboNodes ? is an innovative solution to reduce and reuse the energy , while eliminating the on-site support staff . <p> In today 's data centers , cold air is pumped into the server room and thousands of small fans in the servers are moving the air thought the servers . The hot air coming out of the server is lost by mixing with the cold air . In better cases there are cold&amp;hot isles , but it is still far from being efficient . <p> " The server rack is more than 50 years old . " said Szabo . " There is no other piece of technology in data centers that has survived for so long . " <p> RoboNodes consist of custom server racks and servers . The air used for cooling is completely separated from the air in the server room , which means we capture all of the resulting heat that we can reuse for heating the building or recovering back to electricity . @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ @ valves , which guarantees that no server is being cooled more than necessary . <p> In case of a server failure , the whole server is replaced by an autonomous robotized vehicle as shown in the video . This removes the need of 24/7 staff on site and allows for small autonomous data centers to be spread to many locations . RoboNodes data centers could be also deployed in cold remote areas and managed remotely . <p> " We are the global leader in pay-as-you-go web hosting , which means we need a lot of supporting IT architecture " said Szabo . " Working with commodity HW is often painful and inefficient . The idea for the RoboNodes therefore came from the need of more efficient IT infrastructure . Our web hosting cost just around $1/mo , this constantly drives us to achieve better efficiencies . "

Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon will be pressing governments to speedily ratify the historic agreement on climate change reached in December . <p> Segolene Royal told reporters after meeting the U.N . chief on Wednesday that they want the agreement ratified by the time the parties to global climate talks that led to the Paris agreement hold their next meeting in Marrakesh , Morocco from Nov. 7-18 . <p> The agreement will enter into force once 55 countries representing at least 55 per cent of global emissions have formally joined it . <p> Ban said Tuesday that he is inviting countries to deposit their ratifications on Sept. 21 during the annual ministerial meeting of the General Assembly .
